name: AI in Signal Detection and Its Governance
blurb: Using AI to find new safety signals, and how to govern it.
title: AI in Signal Detection and Its Governance
answer: Beyond case processing, AI helps detect safety signals in large spontaneous report databases and real world data. Published governance work argues these tools should be validated like any GxP system, monitored for data drift and documented so decisions can be explained to regulators.

reading.body:
AI in signal detection should widen what reviewers see, not decide what counts as a signal, with the human assessment and its rationale kept on record.

The governance pattern here is that signal detection is treated as a regulated function rather than a modelling exercise. A 2024 review in PMC set out the terms: GxP style validation, ongoing monitoring for data drift, and documentation complete enough that decisions can be explained to regulators. The EMA reflection paper from September 2024 lists signal detection among the uses of AI regulators expect across the medicine lifecycle, which puts the activity inside the same expectations as the rest of the lifecycle rather than in a separate experimental lane.

For AI specifically, the constraint is not the scale of the spontaneous report database or the real world data. It is that a signal is a judgement with a regulatory consequence, so the tool has to be validated and monitored like any GxP system, and its output has to survive an explanation to an inspector. That is why the human signal assessment stays in the loop and its rationale stays on record.

The data covers governance positions and regulator expectations, not performance. It gives no measured sensitivity or specificity for any detection method, no count of signals found or missed, and no comparison against existing statistical methods. It also does not say how validation is carried out in practice or who signs it off.

explainer:
A safety signal is information suggesting a new possible link between a medicine and an adverse event, or a new aspect of a known one, that warrants investigation. Signal detection traditionally uses statistical methods on spontaneous report databases, looking for drug and event combinations reported more often than expected.

AI adds the ability to combine many data sources, including real world records and literature, to detect patterns in narratives, and to prioritise which statistical alerts deserve attention. The governance challenge is that signal decisions carry regulatory weight. Tools should be validated, monitored for drift as reporting patterns change, and documented so that the reasoning behind each decision can be explained. The final assessment of whether a signal is real, and what action to take, remains with qualified safety physicians and committees.
